title: Animal and human bites | NHS inform
text:
Animal and human bites
Most animal or human bites are not serious but you may need treatment if there are signs of infection.
Symptoms of animal and human bites
Animal and human bites, including bites from a cat or dog, may:
cut the skin
cause bleeding
be painful
leave objects from the bite in the skin, like teeth, hair or dirt
Sometimes a bite may become infected. This can cause symptoms like:
redness, swelling and heat around the wound
increasing pain
liquid or pus coming the wound
a
fever
of 38C (100.4F) or above
sweats and chills
swollen glands
under the chin or in the neck, armpits or groin
red streaks extending along the skin from the wound
Phone 999 or go to A&E if:
You’ve been bitten by an animal or person and:
the wound is large or deep
you were bitten on your face or head
you can’t stop the bleeding
Phone 111 if:
You’ve been bitten and:
you think there may still be objects like teeth, hair or dirt in the wound
the bite is hot or swollen (it may also be painful, red or darker than the surrounding skin)
you have a high temperature
fluid is leaking from the bite
the bite smells unpleasant
you were bitten on your hands or feet
you were bitten by a person
Treatment for animal and human bites
If you have been bitten by an animal or a human, a healthcare professional will check the wound. They may:
clean the bite and remove any damaged tissue
give you
antibiotics
to help prevent infection
check your risk of getting
tetanus
or
rabies
– they’ll give you treatments to prevent these if needed
close the wound with stitches, sticky strips or special glue, or leave it open to heal
If you’ve been bitten by a person, you may also be offered a blood test to check for
hepatitis B
,
hepatitis C
and
HIV
.
What to do after an animal or human bite
There are some things you can do after an animal or human bite.
Do
clean the wound immediately with running water
use running water to try and remove any objects in the bite like teeth, hair or dirt
squeeze the wound gently so it bleeds slightly (unless it’s already bleeding) – this can help reduce the risk of infection
press a clean cloth over the wound if it’s bleeding heavily
gently pat the wound dry and cover it with a clean dressing after you’ve washed it
take
paracetamol
or
ibuprofen
to ease any pain or swelling – children under 16 years old shouldn’t take aspirin
If the bite has torn off a body part like a finger or ear, wrap it in clean tissue and put it in a plastic bag. Put some ice around the bag and take it with you to hospital.
What causes animal and human bites?
Animals can act unpredictably and there isn’t always a reason why they bite. However, an animal is more likely to bite if it’s been disturbed, feels threatened or gets overexcited.
You may be more worried about bites from wild and stray animals but any animal has the potential to bite. Many bites are caused by pets or an animal belonging to a friend or neighbour.
Human bites can happen for different reasons, including during contact sports.
How to prevent animal and human bites
Don’t
do not leave young children alone with any animal
do not approach animals suddenly
do not approach animals when they’re sleeping
do not touch or get too close to unfamiliar dogs or animals
It’s also a good idea to avoid contact with any wild or stray animals, particularly while travelling abroad. They can be aggressive and may carry infections.
Complications of animal and human bites
Some animal and human bites can get infected. These infections aren’t usually serious if they’re treated quickly.
Sometimes an infection can spread to the blood or other parts of the body.
Serious infections like
tetanus
and
rabies
are very rare in the UK.
